sections.overview: Papilio clytia, the Common Mime, is an Asian swallowtail whose patterned forms resemble distasteful butterflies. Some regional sources use the genus Chilasa for this species.
sections.identification: Adults are bluish black with pale streaks and marginal spots; the underside has yellow spots on the hindwing. Two main forms occur: a brown pattern and a contrasting black-and-white striped pattern.
sections.habitat: It ranges across South and Southeast Asia. In Singapore, records include forests as well as parks and gardens.
sections.diet: Caterpillars feed on host plants including Cinnamomum iners; host records vary among local accounts. Adults visit flowers for nectar.
sections.behavior: Both sexes can show either principal wing pattern. These forms imitate distasteful danaine butterflies, including tiger and crow butterflies, which may deter predators.
sections.reproduction: Females lay eggs on host plants; the larva passes through caterpillar and pupal stages before emerging as an adult. The sources consulted do not establish a single development time for the species.
sections.ecology: Its mimicry is notably variable for a swallowtail because both sexes can express alternate patterns. It belongs to the swallowtail family Papilionidae.
sections.conservation: A Singapore government account calls it common locally. This local status is not a global conservation assessment, which was not located in the sources consulted.
